answer: The unemployment rate was 4.2% in September 2026. BLS published it in the Employment Situation report on October 2, 2026.

Headline CPI-U rose about 3.4% year over year in August 2026, seasonally adjusted. I calculated this from FRED's CPIAUCSL index (334.131 in Aug 2026 against 323.291 in Aug 2025, which works out to 3.35%). BLS's own 12-month figure for August 2026 is also 3.4%, but BLS states it on an unadjusted basis. That report came out September 11, 2026, and the September CPI is due October 14, 2026.
Total nonfarm payrolls rose by 29,000 (seasonally adjusted) in September 2026. BLS published this on October 2, 2026.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% in the week of October 1, 2026, up from 7.03% the week before. Source: Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey.
The 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield was 3.85% on October 2, 2026, the latest observation available. Source: Federal Reserve H.15, series DGS10, as shown on FRED.
The monthly effective federal funds rate averaged 3.75% in September 2026, up from 3.63% in August. Source: Federal Reserve, series FEDFUNDS, as shown on FRED.
Real GDP grew at a 2.2% annualized rate in Q2 2026. This is BEA's third estimate, released September 30, 2026. The Q3 2026 advance estimate is due October 29, 2026.

Housing starts ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,275,000 units in August 2026, down from 1,309,000 in July. The figure comes from the Census Bureau/HUD New Residential Construction report released September 17, 2026, but I read the number on FRED (series HOUST) because the Census page excerpt did not show it.
Initial jobless claims were 197,000 (seasonally adjusted) for the week ending September 26, 2026. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, series ICSA, as shown on FRED.

The University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment was 48.1 in September 2026, which is the final reading. FRED's UMCSENT series still shows August (51.7) as its latest point, because FRED posts the index a month late.
The U.S. unemployment rate in April 2020 was 14.8% (seasonally adjusted). That is the current revised figure. BLS first reported 14.7%. Source: BLS, via FRED series UNRATE.
The U.S. unemployment rate in October 2009 was 10.0% (seasonally adjusted), the peak of the Great Recession period. Source: BLS, via FRED series UNRATE.

The highest weekly 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 1981 was 18.63%, in the week of October 9, 1981. It is also the all-time high of the survey. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, via FRED series MORTGAGE30US.
The 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield on March 9, 2020 was 0.54%. It had been 0.74% on March 6 and was 0.76% on March 10. Source: Federal Reserve Board H.15, via FRED series DGS10.

Year-over-year headline CPI inflation in June 2022 was about 9.0%, using the seasonally adjusted CPI-U index (294.957 in June 2022 against 270.654 in June 2021, which works out to 8.98%). BLS's headline figure, which uses the non-seasonally-adjusted index, was 9.1%. Source: BLS, via FRED series CPIAUCSL. The percentage is my calculation from the index levels.

Housing starts in January 2006 were 2,273,000 units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (2,273 thousand). That was the housing-boom peak. Source: U.S. Census Bureau/HUD New Residential Construction, via FRED series HOUST.

The lowest monthly reading of the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index in 2022 was 50.0, in June 2022. It was the record low for the series. Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, via FRED series UMCSENT.

The WTI crude oil spot price (Cushing, OK) on April 20, 2020 was -$36.98 per barrel. That is negative, the first negative price on record. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, via FRED series DCOILWTICO.

The U.S. personal saving rate in April 2020 was 31.8% of disposable personal income (seasonally adjusted annual rate), in the current revised data. Earlier vintages showed different values, such as 33.7% at first release. Source: BEA, via FRED series PSAVERT.

Real GDP in Q2 2020 fell at a -28.0% seasonally adjusted annualized rate, in the current revised data. Earlier estimates were larger: -32.9% at the advance estimate and later -31.4%. Source: BEA, via FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA.
The effective federal funds rate averaged 19.04% in July 1981 (monthly average, not seasonally adjusted). Source: Federal Reserve Board, via FRED series FEDFUNDS.
The median sales price of houses sold in the U.S. was $442,600 in Q4 2022 (quarterly, not seasonally adjusted). Source: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD, via FRED series MSPUS.

The unemployment rate averaged about 3.7% in 2019. The 12 seasonally adjusted monthly rates sum to 44.1, which gives 3.675%. Monthly rates ran from 4.0% in January to 3.5% in September. Source: BLS, via FRED series UNRATE.

Five months: January through May 2023. Year-over-year CPI-U inflation (seasonally adjusted index) was about 6.3% in January, 6.0% in February, 4.9% in March, 5.0% in April and 4.1% in May, then 3.1% in June. It stayed between about 3.0% and 3.7% for the rest of the year. These rates were computed from the index levels. Source: BLS, via FRED series CPIAUCSL.
The highest weekly 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 2023 was 7.79%, in the week ending October 26, 2023. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, via FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

The U.S. added about 1,459,000 nonfarm payroll jobs from December 2023 to December 2024. Payrolls went from 156,857 thousand to 158,316 thousand, seasonally adjusted. These are current vintage figures after benchmark revisions, which are well below the roughly 2.2 million first reported in January 2025. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, via FRED series PAYEMS.

The index rose about 129.6% from January 2012 to June 2022, from 134.157 to 308.055 (Jan 2000 = 100, not seasonally adjusted). Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index), via FRED series CSUSHPINSA.

The most negative daily 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread in 2023 was -1.08 percentage points, on July 3, 2023. The next lowest were -1.07 on March 8, 2023 and -1.06 on June 30, 2023. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, via FRED series T10Y2Y (constant-maturity yields from the Federal Reserve H.15 release).

Three quarters: 2020 Q1 (-5.2%), 2020 Q2 (-28.0%) and 2022 Q1 (-1.0%), measured as seasonally adjusted annualized real GDP growth. In current data 2022 Q2 is +0.6%, although it was first reported as negative. Source: BEA, via FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA.

Initial jobless claims peaked at 6,137,000 in the week ending April 4, 2020 (seasonally adjusted, current revised data). The week ending March 28, 2020 was 5,946,000. When first released, the peak was reported as about 6.87 million for the week ending March 28; later seasonal-factor revisions moved it. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, via FRED series ICSA.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, April 4, 2025): +228,000 jobs in March 2025 (nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted). The current data (FRED PAYEMS, updated October 2, 2026, after later monthly and benchmark revisions) puts payrolls at 158,310k in February 2025 and 158,377k in March 2025, a gain of about +67,000. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, read through FRED and the ALFRED vintage for April 4, 2025.

First reported (BLS, June 6, 2025): +139,000 jobs in May 2025 (nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted). The current data (FRED PAYEMS, updated October 2, 2026) puts payrolls at 158,485k in April 2025 and 158,498k in May 2025, a gain of about +13,000. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, read through FRED and ALFRED.

First reported (BLS, July 3, 2025): +147,000 jobs in June 2025 (nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted). The current data (FRED PAYEMS, updated October 2, 2026) puts payrolls at 158,498k in May 2025 and 158,478k in June 2025, a loss of about -20,000 jobs. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, read through FRED and ALFRED.

First reported (BLS, August 1, 2025): +73,000 jobs in July 2025 (nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted). The current data (FRED PAYEMS, updated October 2, 2026) puts payrolls at 158,478k in June 2025 and 158,542k in July 2025, a gain of about +64,000. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, read through FRED and ALFRED.

The advance estimate (BEA, April 28, 2022) put real GDP growth for Q1 2022 at -1.4% (seasonally adjusted annual rate). The current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, updated September 30, 2026) shows -1.0%. Source: BEA National Income and Product Accounts, read through FRED and ALFRED.

The advance estimate (BEA, July 28, 2022) put real GDP growth for Q2 2022 at -0.9% (seasonally adjusted annual rate). The current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, updated September 30, 2026) shows +0.6%. Revisions have turned the decline into growth. Source: BEA, read through FRED and ALFRED.

The advance estimate (BEA, January 30, 2025) put real GDP growth for Q4 2024 at 2.3% (seasonally adjusted annual rate). The current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, updated September 30, 2026, after BEA's 2026 annual update) shows 2.4%. Source: BEA, read through FRED and ALFRED.

Using data published by March 1, 2025, the latest U.S. unemployment rate was 4.0% (seasonally adjusted) for January 2025. BLS published it on February 7, 2025; the February figure did not come out until March 7. Source: BLS Current Population Survey (UNRATE), read through the ALFRED vintage as of March 1, 2025.

As of February 1, 2025, total nonfarm employment for December 2024 was 159,536,000 (159,536 thousand, seasonally adjusted). This is the figure from the January 10, 2025 Employment Situation release, before the benchmark revision of February 7, 2025. Today's data shows 158,316 thousand for that month. Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics, read through the ALFRED PAYEMS vintage for January 31, 2025.

As first reported (January 2025 vintage), seasonally adjusted CPI-U was 317.685 for December 2024 and 308.742 for December 2023, giving 2.9% year over year (about 2.90%). The current data (FRED CPIAUCSL, updated September 11, 2026) gives 317.604 and 308.741, still 2.9% (about 2.87%). BLS's headline (not seasonally adjusted) figure for December 2024 was also 2.9%. These are my own calculations from the index levels. Source: BLS CPI, read through FRED and ALFRED.

FRED's 30-year fixed mortgage rate (series MORTGAGE30US) comes from Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey. It is published weekly, with weeks ending Thursday. Units are percent, not seasonally adjusted. The latest figure on the page was 7.28% for the week of October 1, 2026.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED's S&P 500 series (SP500) is the daily closing index value, not seasonally adjusted. FRED keeps only 10 years of daily history: the page says FRED will include 10 years of daily history for S&P and Dow Jones series. That means the copy reaches back about to October 2016, not to the index's 1957 start.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, released as the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices. The FRED series is CSUSHPINSA. It is monthly, indexed to January 2000 = 100, and not seasonally adjusted.
It comes from the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. The FRED series is UMCSENT. It is monthly, indexed to 1966 Q1 = 100, and not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), from its Spot Prices release. The FRED series is DCOILWTICO, the West Texas Intermediate price at Cushing, Oklahoma. It is daily, in dollars per barrel, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration, part of the Department of Labor, from its Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims Report. Yes, the headline series ICSA is seasonally adjusted. It is a count of claims, published weekly with weeks ending Saturday. FRED also carries a not seasonally adjusted version, ICNSA.
Billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, published quarterly. The FRED series is GDPC1 and the source is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The units are an index with base period 1982-1984 = 100. The main FRED series, CPIAUCSL, is monthly and seasonally adjusted. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. A not seasonally adjusted version, CPIAUCNS, uses the same base period.

The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development publish it jointly, in the New Residential Sales release. The FRED series is MSPUS, the Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States, which covers new houses only. It is quarterly, in dollars, not seasonally adjusted. FRED carries no existing-home figure under this name.

It depends on which FRED series you mean. The daily series EFFR comes from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which calculates the rate as a volume-weighted median of overnight federal funds transactions. The commonly used series DFF, which also covers weekends, is credited to the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System through its H.15 Selected Interest Rates release. Both are in percent and not seasonally adjusted. The New York Fed is the original calculator of the rate.
